answer:
The boundary is promising. I would tighten “meaningful linear order” before code, especially “explained stages.” Everything below is design advice, not a Product Owner decision.

My recommended promise is: “Sequence presents supplied items whose relative position communicates a stated relationship. Numbers identify positions within this sequence; connectors express continuity of that relationship—not elapsed time, causation, importance, execution, or completion.”

Evidence and authority: I recovered the September 9, 2026 consultation at @session:default/run_098d17751e00436b987a5298c5e541df. It explicitly classified removing connectors as a proposed response, not a PO requirement. That advice creates no obligation to remove Journey’s numbers or connectors, and your reported newer direction supersedes it.

I could not independently inspect docs/semantic-visual-language.md at c010e7d. Searches under /workspace and /opt/data found no copy; the exact public raw URL returned HTTP 404. Consequently, I treat the current authority and Travis’s newer feedback as supplied context, not independently verified quotations. I found no authoritative constraint in the retrieved material that this proposal would violate; that is not an exhaustive clearance.

The minimum distinctions I would establish before code are these.

Procedure means a supplied order for doing something. Chronology means a supplied temporal order of events. Explained stages needs a narrower definition: either stages in an explicitly described process, or an author-chosen explanatory progression. Those are different claims. “How this process unfolds” must not silently become “the order I chose to explain these topics.” I recommend leaving generic explanatory progression outside the first contract unless its relationship can be stated more precisely.

The adjacent-swap test is useful but insufficient. Priority rankings also fail that test, yet you correctly exclude them. Conversely, a legitimate procedure can contain interchangeable steps. The first contract should not force a strict order onto those steps: group them without internal ordering, if supported, or decline Sequence. The test should be “would swapping misrepresent the stated relationship?” rather than merely “would it change the reading experience?”

Use one relationship across a sequence’s sibling items. A procedure can include supplied dates as detail without becoming chronology. But “incident happened → team should investigate → likely recovery phase” mixes observation, recommendation, and projection. Item wording must preserve those distinctions; a connector cannot make them equivalent. If the connecting relationship itself changes, separate the compositions or decline Sequence.

Linearity must not imply completeness. Establish whether this is a complete procedure, selected events, an excerpt, or one explicitly scoped path. Numbers are local positions, not evidence that no intermediate events or steps exist. A selected chronology can remain chronological across omissions; a procedure with omitted required actions can become misleading. Scope therefore cannot be treated as decorative provenance.

Qualifier placement needs a stronger obligation than “preserve all text.” A qualification belongs with the smallest claim or action it changes, and must be encountered before someone would rely on an unqualified version.

“Estimated” should accompany an estimated time. “Only if approved” belongs in or immediately alongside the action label, not in a trailing shared note. “This service operates one day only” belongs with the relevant service/date claim. A genuinely sequence-wide limitation can sit near the title/context. Shared notes are suitable for common background or source detail, not for hiding exceptions that reverse individual items.

Short labels should therefore be scanable, not forcibly terse. Sometimes “After approval, submit” is the minimum faithful label. Optional detail means absent when unnecessary—not expendable when layout gets crowded. HUD should keep wrapped detail attached to its item and avoid a viewport or truncation treatment that presents a materially qualified action as unconditional. A generic “more below” indicator does not repair that problem.

Keep the numbered connected spine as requested. Its treatment should preserve position and grouping without adding unsupplied semantics: no current-step emphasis, completed markers, proportional time gaps, or progress fill. Chronology may have known timestamps, but ordering alone does not establish duration or causality. Procedure numbering does not establish that anything has run.

Your trial design is sound with one important qualification: freeze the taught contract and entrypoint, not the conclusion that authors ought to select Sequence. The inappropriate case should still contain attractive numbers or apparent order—such as ranked recommendations or tied events—so declining requires semantic judgment rather than spotting an unordered list. Keep the expected rationale outside the author’s packet. Two appropriate cases can test transfer across two relationship kinds; they cannot establish a third untested kind.

I would keep your independent review categories and explicitly check unsupported implications within fidelity: did the composition invent completeness, certainty, necessity, chronology, or status? Selection can be correct while the presentation still makes a false promise.

The consequential unresolved choice for Travis is whether Sequence primarily communicates an order already present in the supplied subject matter, or also an order authored for explanation. My recommendation is the former for this first brief: supplied procedure and chronology, with stages admitted only when the staged relationship itself is supplied and clear. That is a small, teachable boundary—not a production schema or a permanent palette restriction.

No implementation, project, or memory changes were made.
note: Dottie evidence/context, not implementation authorization. No automatic retry.
